individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: This paper proposes SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free token pruning method for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key insight is that consecutive action generations share high visual redundancy, so global information from previous steps can complement local information from the current generation for more reliable token selection. The method combines three components: (1) static token pruning at the action level using global attention scores from previous generations, dynamic token detection via frame comparison, and local attention from early LLM layers; (2) dynamic token pruning at the layer level using rank-based and confidence-based importance scoring with exponential moving average updates; (3) a lightweight action-aware controller that identifies fine-grained vs. coarse-grained actions based on end-effector velocity and adjusts pruning aggressiveness accordingly. Experiments on LIBERO benchmarks with OpenVLA-OFT show average speedups of 1.46× on A800 and 1.57× on RTX 3090 GPUs with negligible success rate degradation (<0.7%).
Strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight about temporal redundancy across consecutive action generations in VLA models
Training-free approach that is practical for deployment without additional fine-tuning
Comprehensive evaluation across four LIBERO task suites and two hardware platforms
Clear ablation study demonstrating the contribution of each technical component
Well-written and organized paper with good contextualization of related work
The action-aware controller provides an interesting adaptive mechanism for balancing speed and accuracy
Weaknesses: Modest speedup gains (1.46×) that are comparable to some baselines (EfficientVLA achieves 1.55×) but with better success rate retention
All experiments are conducted in simulation only; real-world deployment challenges are acknowledged but not addressed
Several hyperparameters (τ, K_D, β, velocity thresholds) appear manually tuned without sensitivity analysis, raising questions about generalizability
The action-aware controller relies on heuristic thresholds that may not transfer well across different robot platforms or task distributions
Limited analysis of the computational overhead of the pruning mechanisms themselves (frame comparison, attention computation for early layers)
The theoretical analysis in the appendix is superficial and does not fully account for the overhead of the pruning process
No comparison with other acceleration techniques like quantization or early exit that could potentially be combined with pruning
Questions: How sensitive are the results to the hyperparameters τ (similarity threshold), K_D (number of dynamic tokens), and β (EMA update rate)? Have you conducted sensitivity analysis for these parameters?

What is the additional computational overhead of the pruning mechanisms themselves (frame comparison, attention computation for the first two layers, velocity-based controller)? How does this overhead factor into the reported end-to-end latency?

The velocity-based frame sampling strategy uses a heuristic formula T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4. How was this formula derived? Does it generalize to different control frequencies or robot platforms?
How do the thresholds for the action-aware controller (v_t^th, v_r^th, v_z^th) scale with different robot arm specifications or action space normalizations?
Could the proposed method be combined with other acceleration techniques such as quantization or KV-cache compression for further speedup? Have you explored such combinations?
The paper reports that EfficientVLA achieves higher speedup but with significant success rate drop on LIBERO-Long. Could you analyze why your method is more robust in this scenario?
How does the pruning ratio α interact with the action-aware controller? Is there an optimal balance between static pruning aggressiveness and dynamic adjustment?

What happens when the environment changes rapidly (e.g., moving objects not related to the task)? Does the dynamic token detection effectively capture these changes without retaining too many irrelevant tokens?
Limitations: All experiments are conducted in simulated environments (LIBERO), and real-world deployment may introduce sensor noise, environmental dynamics, and hardware latency not captured in simulation
The method relies on several heuristic thresholds and manually tuned parameters that may not generalize across different robot platforms, camera setups, or task distributions
The speedup gains are modest (1.46×-1.57×), and the method does not address the vision encoder or action head latency, which may become bottlenecks in different model architectures
The temporal consistency assumption may break down in highly dynamic environments or tasks requiring rapid adaptation to changing goals
No analysis of the memory overhead or energy consumption of the pruning approach
The evaluation is limited to a single VLA model (OpenVLA-OFT); generalizability to other architectures (e.g., diffusion-based action heads) is not demonstrated

individual_reviews.raw_response:
THOUGHT:
This paper proposes SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free token pruning method for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key insight is combining global information from previous action generations with local information from the current generation for token selection. The method includes three components: (1) static token pruning at action level using global attention from previous steps, dynamic token detection via frame comparison, and local attention from early layers; (2) dynamic token pruning at layer level using rank-based and confidence-based importance scoring; (3) a lightweight action-aware controller that adjusts pruning aggressiveness based on action granularity (coarse vs. fine-grained).

The paper addresses a relevant problem (VLA model inference acceleration) and demonstrates meaningful speedups (1.46× on A800, 1.57× on RTX 3090) with negligible success rate loss on LIBERO benchmarks. The temporal redundancy insight across consecutive actions is well-motivated and empirically supported.

Strengths:
- Novel insight combining temporal (global) and current-step (local) information for pruning
- Training-free approach, practical for deployment
- Comprehensive evaluation on multiple benchmarks and hardware platforms
- Good ablation study showing contribution of each component
- Clear writing and well-organized structure

Weaknesses:
- The speedup gains (1.46×) are modest compared to some baselines (EfficientVLA achieves 1.55×)
- Limited evaluation on real-world scenarios (only simulation)
- The action-aware controller adds complexity with heuristic thresholds that may not generalize well
- Some hyperparameters (e.g., τ, K_D, β) appear manually tuned without sensitivity analysis
- The comparison with EfficientVLA shows similar speedup but better success rate retention for the proposed method, but the paper doesn't deeply analyze why
- The theoretical analysis in the appendix is somewhat superficial
- No analysis of memory overhead or additional computational costs of the pruning mechanisms themselves

The paper is technically sound with reasonable experimental validation. The results are meaningful but not groundbreaking. The temporal consistency insight is valuable and could inspire future work. The main concerns are the modest speedup, limited evaluation scope, and potential overfitting of hyperparameters to specific benchmarks.

I would rate this as a borderline accept. The work is solid but not exceptional. The speedup is modest, and while the insight is novel, the practical impact may be limited. The paper would benefit from more thorough analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity and broader evaluation.

THOUGHT:
The paper proposes SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free token pruning method for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key insight is that consecutive action generations share high visual redundancy, so global information from previous generations can be combined with local information from current generation for more reliable token selection. The method has three components: static token pruning at action level using global attention from previous steps, dynamic token pruning at layer level, and a lightweight action-aware controller that adjusts pruning based on action granularity (coarse vs fine).

The paper is well-motivated with clear profiling showing LLM is the bottleneck. The experiments on LIBERO benchmark show 1.46x speedup on A800 and 1.57x on RTX 3090 with negligible success rate loss. The ablation study confirms each component contributes.

Strengths:
- Novel insight about temporal redundancy across consecutive actions
- Training-free approach, practical for deployment
- Comprehensive evaluation on multiple datasets and hardware
- Good ablation study
- Clear writing and visualization

Weaknesses:
- The speedup is modest (1.46x-1.57x) compared to some baselines
- All experiments in simulation only
- The action-aware controller relies on velocity thresholds that may need tuning per task
- Limited comparison with recent methods (only 3 baselines)
- The dynamic layer pruning seems to add latency (1.6ms) while reducing tokens, raising questions about its efficiency benefit
- The paper claims "self-speculative" but doesn't clearly connect to speculative decoding literature

Overall, this is a solid paper with a practical contribution. The insight about temporal redundancy is interesting and the method is well-engineered. However, the speedup is modest and the evaluation is limited to simulation. I would rate this as a borderline accept - the technical soundness is good but the significance is moderate.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free token pruning method for accelerating Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key insight is that consecutive action generations exhibit high visual similarity, enabling the use of global information from previous actions combined with local information from the current generation for more reliable token selection. The method comprises three components: (1) static token pruning at the action level using attention scores from prior inference, dynamic token detection via frame comparison, and self-speculative selection from early layers; (2) dynamic token pruning at the layer level using importance scores with rank-based weighting and layer confidence across select transformer layers; and (3) a lightweight action-aware controller that categorizes actions as coarse-grained or fine-grained based on end-effector velocity and adjusts pruning aggressiveness accordingly. Experiments on the LIBERO benchmark show an average 1.46× speedup on NVIDIA A800 and 1.57× on RTX 3090 with negligible success rate degradation compared to OpenVLA-OFT.
Strengths: Clear problem motivation with latency breakdown analysis showing LLM backbone as the dominant bottleneck in VLA inference
Novel insight about temporal consistency across consecutive action generations, well-supported by empirical observations (e.g., 85-95% hit rate of top-k tokens between early and final layers)
Well-structured method with three complementary components that address different aspects of token redundancy
Comprehensive evaluation across four LIBERO task suites and two hardware platforms
Training-free approach is practical and can be applied to existing models without fine-tuning
Good ablation study demonstrating the contribution of each component
Includes design space exploration for pruning ratio selection
Weaknesses: Modest speedup (1.46×) compared to some baselines (EfficientVLA achieves 1.55×), and the paper's comparison with EfficientVLA may be unfair since it notes the baseline is designed for diffusion action experts and was re-implemented
Success rate degradation on LIBERO-Long (94.5% to 94.0%) could be significant in safety-critical robotic applications, despite being labeled 'negligible'

The action-aware controller relies on hand-crafted thresholds (v_t^th, v_r^th, v_z^th) and an arbitrary velocity-based frame sampling formula (T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4) that lack clear justification and may not generalize across tasks or environments
Dynamic token pruning is only applied to 4 specific layers (5, 10, 15, 20) with a fixed 10% extra pruning, which seems limited given the claim of 'layer-level' pruning
The term 'self-speculative' is used but the method does not implement actual speculative decoding—it merely uses early layers for token selection, which may be misleading
The FLOPs analysis in the appendix is approximate and does not account for overheads from frame comparison, attention score computation, or the action-aware controller
Lack of real-world validation (acknowledged as a limitation) limits confidence in practical applicability
Questions: How were the thresholds for the action-aware controller (v_t^th, v_r^th, v_z^th) determined? Are they fixed across all LIBERO tasks or tuned per dataset? What is the sensitivity of the method to these values?
Can you provide more detail on the derivation of the velocity-based frame sampling formula T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4? What motivated this specific functional form and coefficients?
Why were layers 5, 10, 15, and 20 chosen for dynamic token pruning? Would applying pruning at more layers improve speedup or hurt accuracy?
What is the computational overhead of the action-aware controller and the frame comparison step? How much of the measured latency includes these components?
How does the method perform with other VLA base models such as CogACT or pi0, which have different architectures and action heads?
The success rate drop on LIBERO-Long is 0.5%—is this statistically significant given the number of trials (40-50 per task)? Could you provide confidence intervals?
In Figure 3(e), the success rate drops sharply when more than 50% of tokens are pruned. What is the maximum safe pruning ratio before performance degrades unacceptably?
How does the method handle cases where the environment changes abruptly (e.g., a new object appears)? Is the dynamic token supplementation sufficient in such scenarios?
Limitations: All experiments are conducted in simulated environments (LIBERO); real-world deployment may introduce sensor noise, environmental dynamics, and hardware latency not captured in simulation
Success rate degradation on long-horizon tasks (LIBERO-Long) suggests the method may not be suitable for all robotic applications, particularly safety-critical ones
The method relies on several hand-crafted heuristics (thresholds, frame sampling formula, layer selection) that may not generalize to diverse tasks and environments without manual tuning
The speedup gains are modest compared to some existing methods, and the practical impact may be limited for applications requiring real-time control with strict latency requirements
The paper does not provide a thorough analysis of failure cases or scenarios where the pruning strategy fails to preserve task-critical information
No evaluation of the method's robustness to different camera viewpoints, lighting conditions, or object appearances beyond the LIBERO benchmark

individual_reviews.raw_response:
THOUGHT:
The paper proposes SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free token pruning method for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key insight is that consecutive action generations share high visual similarity, so global information from previous actions can be combined with local information from the current generation for more reliable token selection. The method has three components: (1) static token pruning at action level using attention scores from previous inference plus dynamic token detection via frame comparison, (2) dynamic token pruning at layer level using importance scores with rank-based weighting and layer confidence, and (3) a lightweight action-aware controller that adjusts pruning aggressiveness based on whether actions are coarse-grained (high velocity) or fine-grained (low velocity, e.g., grasping).

The paper addresses a relevant problem—LLM backbone latency in VLA models is a bottleneck. The idea of leveraging temporal consistency across actions is novel and well-motivated with empirical observations. The method is training-free and achieves 1.46× speedup on A800 and 1.57× on RTX 3090 with negligible success rate loss on LIBERO.

Strengths:
- Clear problem motivation with latency breakdown analysis showing LLM dominance
- Novel insight about temporal redundancy across consecutive actions
- Well-structured method with clear components
- Comprehensive experiments on multiple LIBERO suites and hardware platforms
- Good ablation study showing contribution of each component
- Training-free approach is practical

Weaknesses:
- The speedup is modest (1.46×) compared to some baselines (EfficientVLA achieves 1.55×)
- The success rate on LIBERO-Long drops from 94.5% to 94.0%, which may be concerning for safety-critical applications
- The action-aware controller uses hand-crafted thresholds (v_t^th, v_r^th, v_z^th) and a velocity-based frame sampling formula that seems arbitrary and may not generalize
- The dynamic token pruning at layer level only applies to 4 layers (5,10,15,20) with 10% extra pruning—this seems limited
- The paper claims "negligible loss" but shows up to 0.7% drop in success rate, which could be significant in robotics
- Lack of real-world experiments (acknowledged as limitation)
- The comparison with EfficientVLA is somewhat unfair—they note it's for diffusion action experts and they re-implemented it
- The FLOPs analysis in appendix seems approximate and doesn't account for all overheads
- The "self-speculative" terminology is used but the method doesn't really use speculative decoding—it just uses early layers for token selection

Questions:
1. How were the thresholds (v_t^th, v_r^th, v_z^th) determined? Are they dataset-specific?
2. The velocity-based frame sampling formula T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4 seems arbitrary—can you explain its derivation?
3. Why only 4 layers for dynamic pruning? Would more layers help?
4. What is the actual overhead of the action-aware controller and frame comparison?
5. How does the method perform with different base models (e.g., CogACT)?
6. The success rate drop on LIBERO-Long (0.5%)—is this statistically significant given the number of trials?

Limitations:
- Only simulated environments tested
- Success rate degradation on long-horizon tasks
- Hand-crafted heuristics may not generalize
- Modest speedup compared to some baselines
- No real-world validation

Ethical concerns: None apparent—this is about efficiency optimization for robotic control. No obvious negative societal impacts.

Overall assessment: This is a solid paper with a novel insight and reasonable experimental validation. The method is practical (training-free) and addresses an important problem. However, the speedup gains are modest and the heuristics seem somewhat ad-hoc. The paper would benefit from clearer justification of design choices and more thorough analysis of failure cases. I'd rate this as a borderline accept—the technical soundness is good, the presentation is adequate, but the contribution is moderate given the incremental speedup. I'll go with Overall=6 (Weak Accept) but since the decision field only allows Accept/Reject, I'll choose Accept with the rationale that the paper makes a meaningful contribution to VLA acceleration despite its limitations.

Let me formalize the ratings:
- Originality: 3 (High)—novel temporal insight, but combines known techniques
- Quality: 3 (Good)—sound experiments, but some arbitrary design choices
- Clarity: 3 (Good)—well-organized, but some sections could be clearer
- Significance: 3 (High)—addresses important problem with practical solution
- Soundness: 3 (Good)
- Presentation: 3 (Good)
- Contribution: 3 (Good)
- Overall: 6 (Weak Accept)
- Confidence: 4 (Confident)

review.Summary: This paper proposes SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free token pruning method for accelerating Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key insight is that consecutive action generations share high visual redundancy, enabling global information from previous inference steps to complement local attention from the current generation for more reliable token selection. The method combines three components: (1) static action-level token pruning using global attention scores from previous generations, dynamic token detection via frame comparison, and local attention from early LLM layers; (2) dynamic layer-level token pruning using rank-based and confidence-based importance scoring with exponential moving average updates; and (3) a lightweight action-aware controller that adjusts pruning aggressiveness based on end-effector velocity, distinguishing coarse-grained from fine-grained actions. Experiments on the LIBERO benchmark with OpenVLA-OFT report average speedups of 1.46× on A800 and 1.57× on RTX 3090 GPUs with negligible success rate degradation (<0.7%).
Strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight about temporal redundancy across consecutive action generations in VLA models, supported by empirical observations.
Training-free approach that is practical and can be applied to existing models without fine-tuning.
Comprehensive evaluation across four LIBERO task suites and two hardware platforms (A800 and RTX 3090).
Clear ablation study demonstrating the contribution of each technical component.
The action-aware controller provides an interesting adaptive mechanism for balancing speed and accuracy.
Well-written and organized paper with good contextualization of related work and useful design space exploration.
Weaknesses: Modest speedup gains (1.46×–1.57×) that are comparable to some baselines (e.g., EfficientVLA achieves 1.55×), though with better success rate retention.
All experiments are conducted in simulation (LIBERO) only; real-world deployment challenges (sensor noise, environmental dynamics, hardware latency) are acknowledged but not addressed.

The method relies on several manually tuned hyperparameters (similarity threshold τ, dynamic token count K_D, EMA update rate β, velocity thresholds, pruning ratios per dataset) without sensitivity analysis, raising questions about generalizability.

The action-aware controller and velocity-based frame sampling formula (T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4) appear heuristic and may not transfer across robot platforms, control frequencies, or task distributions.

Limited analysis of the computational overhead of the pruning mechanisms themselves (frame comparison, early-layer attention computation, controller), which may not be fully accounted for in reported latency.
Dynamic layer pruning is applied only to four specific layers with a fixed extra pruning ratio, which seems limited given the claim of 'layer-level' pruning.
The term 'self-speculative' is somewhat misleading; the method uses early layers for token selection but does not implement actual speculative decoding.
No comparison with other acceleration techniques (e.g., quantization, early exit, KV-cache compression) that could potentially be combined with pruning.
The theoretical FLOPs analysis in the appendix is approximate and does not account for pruning overheads.
Questions: How sensitive are the results to hyperparameters such as τ, K_D, β, and the velocity thresholds? Have you conducted a systematic sensitivity analysis?

What is the additional computational overhead of the pruning mechanisms (frame comparison, early-layer attention computation, action-aware controller), and is this included in the reported end-to-end latency?
How was the velocity-based frame sampling formula T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4 derived? Does it generalize to different control frequencies or robot platforms?
How were the velocity thresholds for the action-aware controller determined? Are they fixed across tasks or tuned per dataset?
Could the method be combined with other acceleration techniques such as quantization, early exit, or layer skipping (e.g., EfficientVLA) for further speedup? Have you explored such combinations?
Why were layers 5, 10, 15, and 20 chosen for dynamic token pruning? Would applying pruning at more layers improve speedup or hurt accuracy?
How does the method perform on other VLA base models (e.g., CogACT, pi0) with different architectures and action heads?
How does the method handle scenarios where the environment changes drastically between consecutive frames (e.g., moving objects or viewpoint changes)? Is the dynamic token supplementation sufficient?
What is the memory overhead of storing global attention information from previous inference steps?
Is the success rate drop on LIBERO-Long (0.5%) statistically significant given the number of trials? Could confidence intervals be provided?
Limitations: All experiments are conducted in simulated environments (LIBERO); real-world deployment may introduce sensor noise, environmental dynamics, and hardware latency not captured in simulation.

The method relies on several hand-crafted heuristics (thresholds, pruning ratios, frame sampling formula, layer selection) that may require per-task tuning and may not generalize to diverse robot platforms or task distributions.
The speedup gains are moderate (1.4–1.6×) and may not be sufficient for real-time control applications with strict latency requirements.
The temporal consistency assumption may break down in highly dynamic environments or tasks requiring rapid adaptation to changing goals.
No analysis of memory overhead, energy consumption, or failure cases/error propagation over long horizons.
Evaluation is limited to a single VLA model (OpenVLA-OFT); generalizability to other architectures (e.g., diffusion-based action heads) is not demonstrated.

final_review.Summary: This paper proposes SpecPrune-VLA, a training-free token pruning method for accelerating Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The key insight is that consecutive action generations share high visual redundancy, enabling global information from previous inference steps to complement local attention from the current generation for more reliable token selection. The method combines three components: (1) static action-level token pruning using global attention scores from previous generations, dynamic token detection via frame comparison, and local attention from early LLM layers; (2) dynamic layer-level token pruning using rank-based and confidence-based importance scoring with exponential moving average updates; and (3) a lightweight action-aware controller that adjusts pruning aggressiveness based on end-effector velocity, distinguishing coarse-grained from fine-grained actions. Experiments on the LIBERO benchmark with OpenVLA-OFT report average speedups of 1.46× on A800 and 1.57× on RTX 3090 GPUs with negligible success rate degradation (<0.7%).
Strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight about temporal redundancy across consecutive action generations in VLA models, supported by empirical observations.
Training-free approach that is practical and can be applied to existing models without fine-tuning.
Comprehensive evaluation across four LIBERO task suites and two hardware platforms (A800 and RTX 3090).
Clear ablation study demonstrating the contribution of each technical component.
The action-aware controller provides an interesting adaptive mechanism for balancing speed and accuracy.
Well-written and organized paper with good contextualization of related work and useful design space exploration.
Weaknesses: Modest speedup gains (1.46×–1.57×) that are comparable to some baselines (e.g., EfficientVLA achieves 1.55×), though with better success rate retention.
All experiments are conducted in simulation (LIBERO) only; real-world deployment challenges (sensor noise, environmental dynamics, hardware latency) are acknowledged but not addressed.

The method relies on several manually tuned hyperparameters (similarity threshold τ, dynamic token count K_D, EMA update rate β, velocity thresholds, pruning ratios per dataset) without sensitivity analysis, raising questions about generalizability.

The action-aware controller and velocity-based frame sampling formula (T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4) appear heuristic and may not transfer across robot platforms, control frequencies, or task distributions.

Limited analysis of the computational overhead of the pruning mechanisms themselves (frame comparison, early-layer attention computation, controller), which may not be fully accounted for in reported latency.
Dynamic layer pruning is applied only to four specific layers with a fixed extra pruning ratio, which seems limited given the claim of 'layer-level' pruning.
The term 'self-speculative' is somewhat misleading; the method uses early layers for token selection but does not implement actual speculative decoding.
No comparison with other acceleration techniques (e.g., quantization, early exit, KV-cache compression) that could potentially be combined with pruning.
The theoretical FLOPs analysis in the appendix is approximate and does not account for pruning overheads.
Questions: How sensitive are the results to hyperparameters such as τ, K_D, β, and the velocity thresholds? Have you conducted a systematic sensitivity analysis?

What is the additional computational overhead of the pruning mechanisms (frame comparison, early-layer attention computation, action-aware controller), and is this included in the reported end-to-end latency?
How was the velocity-based frame sampling formula T = floor(-16/3 * v/6 + 22/3) + 4 derived? Does it generalize to different control frequencies or robot platforms?
How were the velocity thresholds for the action-aware controller determined? Are they fixed across tasks or tuned per dataset?
Could the method be combined with other acceleration techniques such as quantization, early exit, or layer skipping (e.g., EfficientVLA) for further speedup? Have you explored such combinations?
Why were layers 5, 10, 15, and 20 chosen for dynamic token pruning? Would applying pruning at more layers improve speedup or hurt accuracy?
How does the method perform on other VLA base models (e.g., CogACT, pi0) with different architectures and action heads?
How does the method handle scenarios where the environment changes drastically between consecutive frames (e.g., moving objects or viewpoint changes)? Is the dynamic token supplementation sufficient?
What is the memory overhead of storing global attention information from previous inference steps?
Is the success rate drop on LIBERO-Long (0.5%) statistically significant given the number of trials? Could confidence intervals be provided?
Limitations: All experiments are conducted in simulated environments (LIBERO); real-world deployment may introduce sensor noise, environmental dynamics, and hardware latency not captured in simulation.

The method relies on several hand-crafted heuristics (thresholds, pruning ratios, frame sampling formula, layer selection) that may require per-task tuning and may not generalize to diverse robot platforms or task distributions.
The speedup gains are moderate (1.4–1.6×) and may not be sufficient for real-time control applications with strict latency requirements.
The temporal consistency assumption may break down in highly dynamic environments or tasks requiring rapid adaptation to changing goals.
No analysis of memory overhead, energy consumption, or failure cases/error propagation over long horizons.
Evaluation is limited to a single VLA model (OpenVLA-OFT); generalizability to other architectures (e.g., diffusion-based action heads) is not demonstrated.
